topic: Sepsis-Induced Organ Dysfunction — When the Cascade Bites
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Critical Care Complex
speakerBio: Dual-trained intensivist and nephrologist who runs the ICU's organ-support programme and teaches the SOFA score as a bedside map of the failing patient.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

It is 03:00 in the ICU. A 64-year-old man admitted 18 hours ago with urosepsis is now on noradrenaline at 0.3 µg/kg/min. His creatinine has doubled, his PaO₂/FiO₂ has fallen to 180, his lactate will not clear, and the nurse notes oozing from every cannula site. You resuscitated the blood pressure hours ago — so why is he getting worse? Because sepsis is not a blood-pressure problem. It is a whole-body endothelial and mitochondrial injury, and tonight we are going to walk the wards of the failing organs, one door at a time.

1 · 🗺️ SOFA — the map of the failing organs

Sepsis-3 defines sepsis as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection, operationalised as a rise in the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score of ≥2 points. SOFA is not a triage tool — it is the organ-dysfunction map that structures this entire lecture. Six systems, each scored 0–4:

SystemMarkerScore 1 → 4 (worsening)
RespiratoryPaO₂/FiO₂<400 → <100 (with support)
CoagulationPlatelets ×10⁹/L<150 → <20
LiverBilirubin µmol/L20–32 → >204
CardiovascularMAP / vasopressor doseMAP <70 → high-dose pressors
CNSGlasgow Coma Scale13–14 → <6
RenalCreatinine / urine output110–170 → >440 or <200 mL/day
Sepsis is a systemic disease that presents one organ at a time. Read the SOFA and you read the whole patient.
💡 Mechanism first

The unifying lesion is endothelial injury. Inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6) degrade the endothelial glycocalyx, open cell junctions, and switch the endothelium to a pro-coagulant, vasodilated, leaky state. Add microvascular thrombosis and mitochondrial dysfunction (cytopathic hypoxia — cells cannot use oxygen even when it arrives) and you have the recipe for every organ failure below. This is why a patient with a normalised blood pressure can still be dying.

2 · 🫘 Septic acute kidney injury — not just "hypoperfusion"

Septic AKI is the commonest organ failure in sepsis (~half of ICU cases) and the one most misunderstood. The old teaching — "the kidney is underperfused, give more fluid" — is largely wrong. Post-mortem and experimental data show that in early septic AKI, total renal blood flow is often normal or even increased.

The real mechanism is a triad:

  • Microcirculatory redistribution — flow is shunted away from the medulla; peritubular capillaries become heterogeneous, with hypoxic patches next to well-perfused ones.
  • Inflammation — filtered and circulating PAMPs/DAMPs are sensed by tubular epithelial cells, which respond by downregulating metabolism and entering a protective "cell-cycle arrest" (the basis of biomarkers TIMP-2 and IGFBP7).
  • Venous congestion — over-resuscitation raises central venous pressure, throttling renal venous outflow. The kidney is a low-compliance encapsulated organ; congestion hurts it as much as hypoperfusion.
⚠️ Fluid is a drug with a ceiling

Chasing oliguria with repeated boluses after the patient is filled raises venous pressure and worsens AKI. Oliguria in established septic AKI is frequently a sign of tubular injury, not a fluid deficit. Assess fluid responsiveness dynamically (passive leg raise, stroke-volume variation) before every bolus.

KDIGO staging — the shared language

StageCreatinineUrine output
11.5–1.9× baseline or ↑≥26.5 µmol/L<0.5 mL/kg/h for 6–12 h
22.0–2.9× baseline<0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥12 h
3≥3.0× baseline, or ≥353.6 µmol/L, or RRT started<0.3 mL/kg/h ≥24 h or anuria ≥12 h

Protect the kidney you have

  • Avoid nephrotoxins: stop NSAIDs and ACE-i/ARBs, minimise iodinated contrast, dose-adjust and level vancomycin and aminoglycosides (or avoid aminoglycosides where alternatives exist).
  • Target MAP ≥65 mmHg — but consider a higher target (80–85) in patients with chronic hypertension (SEPSISPAM showed less RRT in that subgroup).
  • Balanced crystalloids (Hartmann's/Plasma-Lyte) over 0.9% saline — SMART and BaSICS lean toward fewer major kidney events with balanced fluids and away from chloride-rich saline.

When to start RRT — the STARRT-AKI verdict

For years we debated "early vs late" dialysis. STARRT-AKI (2020) settled the routine question: an accelerated strategy gave no survival benefit over a standard (watch-and-wait) strategy, and left more patients dependent on dialysis at 90 days. Combined with ELAIN and IDEAL-ICU, the message is clear.

Start RRT for a problem you can name, not for a number on a chart.
💡 The AEIOU emergencies

Dialyse now for refractory Acidosis, Electrolytes (hyperkalaemia unresponsive to medical therapy), Intoxications, Overload (refractory pulmonary oedema), and Uraemic complications (encephalopathy, pericarditis). Absent these, watchful waiting is safe and often lets the kidney recover on its own.

3 · 🫁 Sepsis-induced ARDS — protect the lung from the ventilator

The septic lung leaks. Cytokine-driven alveolar-capillary injury floods alveoli with proteinaceous fluid → the stiff, heavy, low-compliance "baby lung" of ARDS. The Berlin definition grades it by PaO₂/FiO₂ on ≥5 cmH₂O PEEP: mild (200–300), moderate (100–200), severe (<100).

The single most important intervention is not a drug — it is not injuring the lung further. Ventilator-induced lung injury (volutrauma, barotrauma, atelectrauma, biotrauma) turns a survivable lung injury into multi-organ failure.

ParameterTargetWhy
Tidal volume6 mL/kg predicted body weightARMA/ARDSNet: 6 vs 12 mL/kg cut mortality 40%→31%
Plateau pressure≤30 cmH₂OLimits alveolar overdistension
Driving pressure (Pplat − PEEP)<15 cmH₂OAmato: the variable most strongly linked to survival
PEEPHigher in moderate–severeRecruits, prevents atelectrauma
SpO₂ / PaO₂88–95% / 55–80 mmHgPermissive; avoid hyperoxia
pHPermissive hypercapnia to ~7.20Price of low tidal volumes

For moderate–severe ARDS (P/F <150): prone positioning for ≥16 h/day (PROSEVA cut mortality from 33% to 16%) and early neuromuscular blockade in selected patients. Refractory hypoxaemia → consider veno-venous ECMO (EOLIA/CESAR).

In ARDS the ventilator is both the treatment and the weapon. Small breaths, low driving pressure, and turn them over.

4 · 🫀 Septic cardiomyopathy — the heart the pressors hide

Up to 60% of septic shock patients develop reversible biventricular systolic and/or diastolic dysfunction. Mechanism: circulating myocardial-depressant cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β) plus mitochondrial dysfunction and calcium-handling defects in the cardiomyocyte. The hallmark is a dilated, hypokinetic LV with a reduced ejection fraction that paradoxically carries a better prognosis — dilation preserves stroke volume, and survivors normalise their EF within 7–10 days.

🎯 The counter-intuitive twist

A low EF in septic shock is often protective ventricular dilation. The patients who die are frequently those with a "normal-looking" small, stiff ventricle that cannot augment output. Do not be reassured by a normal EF — assess the whole picture with bedside echo (filling, RV, valves, tamponade).

Management is supportive: optimise preload without overloading, use noradrenaline as the first-line vasopressor, and add an inotrope (dobutamine, or milrinone/levosimendan in selected cases) only when there is persistent hypoperfusion despite adequate MAP and filling. The LeoPARDS trial found levosimendan gave no benefit and more arrhythmia and difficulty weaning ventilation — do not reach for it reflexively.

5 · 🩸 DIC — when clotting eats itself

Sepsis-induced coagulopathy sits on a spectrum ending in disseminated intravascular coagulation. Mechanism: tissue-factor-driven systemic thrombin generation → widespread microvascular fibrin thrombi (organ ischaemia) → consumption of platelets and clotting factors → paradoxical bleeding. Antithrombin and protein C are depleted; the glycocalyx is stripped; fibrinolysis is suppressed (PAI-1). Thrombosis and haemorrhage at the same time.

ISTH overt-DIC score (≥5 = overt DIC)

VariablePoints
Platelets >100 (0) / 50–100 (1) / <50 (2)0–2
Fibrin marker (D-dimer/FDP): no rise (0) / moderate (2) / strong (3)0–3
Prolonged PT: <3 s (0) / 3–6 s (1) / >6 s (2)0–2
Fibrinogen >1 g/L (0) / <1 g/L (1)0–1

Treatment is treat the sepsis — there is no magic anticoagulant. Support with blood products only if bleeding or before a procedure: platelets if <50 and bleeding (<20 prophylactically), FFP for prolonged PT/aPTT with bleeding, cryoprecipitate/fibrinogen if fibrinogen <1.5 g/L. Do not transfuse the number — transfuse the bleeding patient.

⚠️ Purpura fulminans

Retiform purpura with acral necrosis in a septic patient (classically meningococcaemia) signals severe DIC with protein C depletion. It is a dermatological emergency demanding aggressive source control and haematology input — the skin is showing you the microthrombosis happening in every organ.

6 · 🫄 Shock liver & hepatic dysfunction

The liver plays two roles in sepsis and can fail in two ways:

  • Hypoxic hepatitis ("shock liver"): after a period of hypoperfusion/hypoxaemia, centrilobular (zone 3) necrosis produces a dramatic transaminase spike into the thousands with a rising LDH, typically 24–72 h after the insult. If perfusion is restored, transaminases fall rapidly over days. A rising bilirubin and INR signal true synthetic failure.
  • Sepsis-associated cholestasis: cytokine-mediated downregulation of bile-acid transporters gives a cholestatic, hyperbilirubinaemic picture out of proportion to the transaminases — the bilirubin drives the SOFA liver score.

Management is restoring perfusion and treating sepsis; avoid hepatotoxins, adjust hepatically-cleared drug doses, and watch for hypoglycaemia and coagulopathy from synthetic failure.

7 · 🧠 Sepsis-associated encephalopathy

Delirium is the brain's SOFA point and the earliest organ dysfunction — present in up to 70% of severe sepsis, often before hypotension. Mechanism: blood–brain-barrier breakdown, neuroinflammation, altered neurotransmission, and microcirculatory dysfunction — not direct CNS infection. It is diffuse (a global confusion, myoclonus, asterixis), and the EEG shows non-specific slowing.

⚠️ It is a diagnosis of exclusion

Before you label a septic patient "just encephalopathic," exclude hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, hyponatraemia, drug effects (sedatives, opioids), non-convulsive status epilepticus, and — critically — meningitis/encephalitis and stroke. New focal signs are never sepsis-associated encephalopathy.

Management: treat the sepsis, remove deliriogenic drugs (benzodiazepines especially), non-pharmacological delirium bundles (orientation, sleep, early mobility), and light sedation targets. Sepsis-associated encephalopathy independently predicts mortality and long-term cognitive impairment — it is a marker of a sick brain, not a benign inconvenience.

8 · 🧪 Adrenal axis & CIRCI

Critical-illness-related corticosteroid insufficiency (CIRCI) is a functional, tissue-level glucocorticoid inadequacy — impaired cortisol production, altered metabolism, and tissue glucocorticoid resistance — relative to the massive demand of critical illness. Random cortisol and the short Synacthen test perform poorly here and are not recommended to guide therapy.

Surviving Sepsis 2021: in septic shock with an ongoing requirement for vasopressors (e.g. noradrenaline/adrenaline ≥0.25 µg/kg/min for ≥4 h), give IV hydrocortisone 200 mg/day (50 mg q6h or infusion). Evidence: APROCCHSS (hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone) showed a mortality benefit; ADRENAL showed no mortality difference but faster shock reversal, fewer transfusions and quicker ICU discharge. The consistent signal is faster shock resolution.

Steroids in sepsis buy time off the pressors — give them to the patient who won't come off noradrenaline, not to everyone with a low blood pressure.
☠️ M&M — the creatinine everyone watched rise

A 58-year-old woman with biliary sepsis was resuscitated to a MAP of 68 and admitted to the ward. Over the next two days she made 15 mL/h of urine. The team, anchored on "she's still dry," gave four more litres of 0.9% saline and 40 mg of gentamicin daily "to cover Gram-negatives," never checking a level. Her CVP climbed to 18, her JVP was to the ear, and her creatinine tripled. By the time nephrology saw her she had a hyperchloraemic acidosis, congestive renal failure, and gentamicin toxicity — and needed three weeks of dialysis. Lessons: oliguria in established septic AKI is usually tubular injury, not hypovolaemia; venous congestion from over-resuscitation is a nephrotoxin; chloride-rich saline and unmonitored aminoglycosides pour fuel on the fire. The kidney she started with was salvageable — the management was not.

9 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Sepsis is endothelial and mitochondrial injury — a normal blood pressure does not mean healthy organs. Read the SOFA.
  2. Septic AKI is inflammation + microcirculatory failure + congestion, not simple hypoperfusion — don't drown it, avoid nephrotoxins, and let STARRT-AKI guide RRT timing (start for AEIOU, not a number).
  3. The ventilator can kill the ARDS lung — 6 mL/kg PBW, Pplat ≤30, driving pressure <15, prone the P/F <150.
  4. Septic cardiomyopathy is reversible and a low EF may be protective — inotropes only for proven hypoperfusion; skip levosimendan.
  5. DIC clots and bleeds at once — treat the source, transfuse the bleeding patient not the ISTH number.
  6. Shock liver spikes transaminases into the thousands and recovers with perfusion; cholestasis drives the bilirubin.
  7. New confusion is often the first organ to fail — but exclude the mimics before calling it encephalopathy.
  8. Give hydrocortisone 200 mg/day to the vasopressor-dependent patient (APROCCHSS/ADRENAL) — it speeds shock reversal.

moderatorQs.q: A septic patient is oliguric despite a normalised MAP and 5 litres of fluid. Do you give more fluid?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: No — not without proving fluid responsiveness first. In established septic AKI, oliguria usually reflects tubular injury and microcirculatory redistribution, not a filling deficit, and total renal blood flow is often normal or high. More fluid after the patient is filled raises central venous pressure and causes renal venous congestion, which worsens the AKI. I would assess dynamically (passive leg raise, stroke-volume variation); if not fluid-responsive, I stop chasing the urine output, target MAP ≥65 (higher if chronically hypertensive, per SEPSISPAM), remove nephrotoxins, and consider whether venous congestion needs decongestion rather than more volume.

moderatorQs.q: How does STARRT-AKI change when you start renal replacement therapy?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: STARRT-AKI (2020) compared an accelerated versus a standard (watchful-waiting) RRT strategy in critically ill AKI and found no mortality benefit to starting early — and the accelerated arm had more 90-day dialysis dependence and more adverse events. With ELAIN and IDEAL-ICU, the consolidated message is: in the absence of a hard indication, wait and let the kidney recover. Start RRT for the AEIOU emergencies — refractory Acidosis, Electrolyte derangement (hyperkalaemia), Intoxication, fluid Overload, and Uraemic complications — a problem you can name, not a creatinine threshold.

moderatorQs.q: You find an EF of 30% on bedside echo in septic shock. Should you start an inotrope?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Not on the number alone. A depressed EF in septic shock usually represents reversible septic cardiomyopathy with protective ventricular dilation, and it typically normalises within 7–10 days — a low EF here often carries a better prognosis than a small, stiff, normal-EF ventricle. I add an inotrope such as dobutamine only when there is persistent tissue hypoperfusion (rising lactate, poor capillary refill, low ScvO₂) despite an adequate MAP and optimised filling. I would not reach for levosimendan — LeoPARDS showed no benefit and more arrhythmia and harder ventilator weaning.

audienceQs.q: What exactly are the lung-protective ventilation targets in sepsis-induced ARDS?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Set the ventilator to protect, not just to oxygenate. Tidal volume 6 mL/kg predicted body weight (calculated from height and sex, not actual weight) — the ARDSNet/ARMA target that cut mortality from 40% to 31%. Keep plateau pressure ≤30 cmH₂O and, most importantly, driving pressure (Pplat − PEEP) <15 cmH₂O — Amato showed this is the mechanical variable most tightly linked to survival. Accept permissive hypercapnia to a pH ~7.20 and target SpO₂ 88–95%. For P/F <150, add prone positioning ≥16 h/day (PROSEVA halved mortality).

audienceQs.q: Which patient with septic shock should get steroids, and what dose?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Give IV hydrocortisone 200 mg/day (as 50 mg every 6 hours or a continuous infusion) to the patient with septic shock and an ongoing vasopressor requirement — Surviving Sepsis 2021 suggests a trigger of noradrenaline/adrenaline ≥0.25 µg/kg/min for at least 4 hours. Do not use a random cortisol or short Synacthen test to decide — they don't perform in CIRCI. The evidence is APROCCHSS (mortality benefit with added fludrocortisone) and ADRENAL (faster shock reversal, fewer transfusions, earlier ICU discharge). It is for the pressor-dependent patient, not everyone who is hypotensive.

audienceQs.q: A septic patient's ALT is 3,000. Is this fulminant liver failure?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Usually not — this pattern is classic hypoxic hepatitis ("shock liver"): centrilobular necrosis after a period of hypoperfusion or hypoxaemia, giving a dramatic transaminase spike into the thousands with a raised LDH, typically 24–72 h after the insult. The reassuring part is that once perfusion is restored the transaminases fall rapidly over a few days. What you actually watch are the markers of synthetic function — a rising bilirubin and INR, and hypoglycaemia — which signal true liver failure. Treat the sepsis, restore perfusion, stop hepatotoxins, and adjust hepatically-cleared drug doses.
